Expected.why: Transient failures such as a 503 are now returned on the first attempt without any retry, while permanently rejected deliveries are retried five times with backoff.

Finding.Comment: The retry decision in `Deliver` is inverted relative to the original `if !retryable(err) { return err }` and to the function's own contract ("A transient failure is retried with exponential backoff, a permanent one is returned at once"). As written, `retryable(lastErr)` is true for every non-permanent error (it is defined as `!errors.Is(err, ErrPermanent)`), so any transient failure — a 503 from the webhook, a temporary network error from `d.client.Do` — returns immediately with the first error and never reaches the retry/backoff loop. Conversely, a permanent rejection (`ErrPermanent`, e.g. a 4xx from the endpoint) is retried up to `maxAttempts` times with sleeps even though the doc comment and the wrapping in `post` say it must be returned at once.
Finding.Headline: Retry condition inverted: transient errors return immediately
Evidence: backoff, a permanent one is returned at once. It returns nil as soon as

Findings.Comment: Replaces the caller-supplied `ctx` with `context.Background()` in both the request construction and the `getTextCapped` call, so the caller's deadline/cancellation no longer bounds the operation — directly contradicting the doc comment on line 10 ("The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read"). On a realistic path where the caller cancels (request timeout, shutdown, user abort), the HTTP request and body read keep running to completion or the transport timeout, so a slow Bitbucket diff holds the connection and memory alive after the caller has given up. The `ctx` parameter is now unused. Both call sites need `ctx` restored — line 13 and the `getTextCapped` call at line 18.
Findings.Headline: Caller context replaced with context.Background, dropping cancellation
Findings.Suggestion: req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u, nil)
Evidence: // The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read.

Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.
Touch now takes milliseconds, so a hold of two hours sets a lifetime of 7.2 seconds and the session expires while the export it was meant to cover is still running.

Finding.Comment: `Hold` passes a seconds count into `Touch`, whose parameter is now `ttlMillis` and is forwarded to `Redis.PExpire` (millisecond TTL). Calling `Hold(ctx, id, 30*time.Minute)` computes `int64(d.Seconds()) == 1800`, so the session TTL becomes 1800ms (~1.8s) instead of 30 minutes — the session dies mid-export. Any `d` under one second truncates to 0 and is rejected by `Touch`'s non-positive TTL check, so short holds fail outright. The rest of the manager was migrated to `idle.Milliseconds()` but this call site still uses seconds.
Finding.Headline: Hold passes seconds to a millisecond TTL API, expiring sessions far too early
Evidence: PExpire(ctx context.Context, key string, ttlMillis int64) (existed bool, err error)

Findings.Comment: `transfer.sourceAccountId()` and `requesterAccountId` are boxed `Long`s, so `!=` compares object identity, not value. Account IDs come back from the repository as freshly allocated `Long` instances (and any id > 127 falls outside the boxing cache), so a legitimate cancellation for, say, account 5001 will pass `transfer.sourceAccountId() != requesterAccountId` as true and throw `TransferAccessDeniedException` even though the requester is the source account. The nearby `create` method already uses `sourceAccountId.equals(targetAccountId)` for the same class of comparison, so this is also inconsistent with the surrounding pattern.
Findings.Headline: Compare source account id with equals, not reference inequality

Expected.why: Boxed Longs are compared by reference, so for any account id above 127 the owner's own cancellation is rejected as access denied.

Findings.Comment: The `defer r.mu.Unlock()` was replaced with an explicit `r.mu.Unlock()` at the tail of the function, but the early-return path for an unknown team still returns while holding the lock. Calling `Disable("no-such-team", "...")` takes `r.mu` at the top of the function, hits `return fmt.Errorf("unknown team %q", slug)` before reaching the unlock, and leaves the mutex locked forever. Every subsequent `Registry` operation that acquires `mu` then blocks indefinitely, so one bad slug wedges the whole registry. Keeping the deferred unlock (or unlocking before the early return) preserves the previous behavior.
Findings.Headline: Early return in Disable leaks the registry lock

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: The `r.Ticket == nil` branch used to return early, but it now only holds a comment and execution falls through to `r.Ticket.Key`. On the documented "ticket is optional" path — any `Result` with a nil `Ticket` — this dereferences a nil pointer and panics instead of returning the body alone.
Findings.Headline: Nil Ticket dereference in Summarize after removing early return
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Expected.why: The nil branch no longer returns, so r.Ticket.Key panics whenever Ticket is nil. A reviewer may anchor on the dead check (19) or on the dereference (22).

The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: Removing `defer resp.Body.Close()` means `WhoAmI` never closes the response body. On every call — including the non-2xx path at `resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode > 299` and the JSON decode path — the body is left open and unread. The caller only receives `*User`, so no one else can close it either. Under repeated use this leaks connections and file descriptors: Go's `http.Client` cannot return the connection to the pool and the body stays open until GC finalizes it, eventually exhausting sockets in a long-running process.
Findings.Headline: Response body never closed after http.Do in WhoAmI

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: This change drops the `q.mu` lock around `q.depth = len(q.pending)`, so the worker goroutine now writes `q.depth` (and reads `q.pending`) with no synchronization while `Submit` and `Depth` both touch those fields under `q.mu`. With a review running and a concurrent `Submit(...)`/`Depth()` call — exactly the scenario `Queue` exists for — this is a data race: `go test -race` will flag it, and `Depth()` can observe a torn or stale backlog value instead of the count the doc comment promises. Restore the lock/unlock pair so every access to `q.depth`/`q.pending` is guarded by the same mutex.
Findings.Headline: Worker updates q.depth without holding q.mu

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.
The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: This hunk replaces the error-checked `tx.Commit(ctx)` with a bare `tx.Commit(ctx)` whose return value is discarded, then unconditionally returns `nil`. A commit can genuinely fail after the `INSERT` succeeded — e.g. the PostgreSQL connection drops between the insert and the COMMIT, or the server aborts the transaction — and in that case `AddClaim` reports success to the caller even though no `team_claims` row was persisted. Any caller that treats a nil error as "the team now owns the project" will silently lose the claim with no retry signal.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim ignores tx.Commit error and always reports success

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
